h1: Craft beer market trends in India
title: Craft Beer Market Trends in India | Craft Beer School
desc: The directions India's craft beer market has been moving: taprooms, cans, regional growth and what a founder should actually watch for.
teaser: The Indian craft beer market has been shifting for years, mostly quietly, mostly in the same few directions.
standfirst: Rather than chase a single headline number, it helps a founder to know the direction things have been moving: which cities, which formats, which channels. Here is the shape of it.
sections: Craft beer in India grew first in a handful of large metros, Bengaluru, Pune, Mumbai and Delhi NCR among them, where a critical mass of drinkers, disposable income and permissive local excise policy came together in a way that smaller markets could not yet match. That pattern has been extending into tier-2 cities as state policy and local demand catch up, though the pace and rules differ sharply by state, which keeps this an uneven national picture rather than a single, tidy trend line.
Taprooms and brewpubs as the entry model

Most small Indian craft breweries have started as brewpubs or taprooms, on-trade first, because it lowers the packaging investment needed to launch and lets a founder build a local following before facing off-trade competition on a crowded shelf full of established brands. This mirrors what is covered in on-trade versus off-trade, and it remains the more common route into the market than launching straight into retail distribution.

More Indian craft breweries packaging for retail have been choosing cans over bottles, for the practical reasons covered in cans versus bottles: better protection from light and heat in transit, lower shipping weight, and increasingly efficient recycling infrastructure across major Indian cities. Bottles have not disappeared, particularly for premium positioning, but the retail packaging shift has been real and fairly consistent across the market.

Early Indian craft brewing leaned heavily on approachable wheat beers and pale ales suited to a market still discovering the category and unfamiliar with more assertive flavours. As drinkers' palates develop, more breweries have introduced hazy IPAs, sours and stronger, more assertive styles, though mainstream lagers and easy-drinking ales still make up the bulk of volume sold across the country.

A founder entering the space should not assume the market has fully moved past accessible styles, most of the volume has not, whatever the more visible craft-focused cities might suggest.
What this means for a new founder

Study your specific city or state's actual excise and licensing environment rather than a national trend line, since state policy differences matter more to your business than the aggregate direction of the market as a whole. Watch the metros for style and packaging direction, but plan your first eighteen months around the on-trade, taproom-first pattern that has worked repeatedly, unless your specific state and site genuinely favour a different route.

See funding a brewery for how these market realities shape what investors actually want to see in a pitch.
Where imported beer and craft beer actually compete

Small Indian craft breweries mostly do not compete head-on with imported beer brands, since imports tend to sit at a different price point and reach a different, smaller slice of drinkers looking specifically for a familiar international name. The more direct competition for a new craft brewery is usually other local craft producers and the mainstream domestic lager brands fighting for the same shelf space and tap handles in the same city.

Understanding who you are actually competing against locally matters more than tracking the broader import market, which rarely determines whether your own brewery succeeds in its own city.

Spend time in the bars and shops you hope to sell into and note what is actually selling, at what price and to whom, rather than relying purely on what national commentary suggests the market wants.

Talk directly to bar owners and shopkeepers about what moves and what sits on the shelf, since their honest answer is usually more reliable than any national trend report, and it costs nothing beyond the conversation itself. Revisit this local picture every few months rather than once, since a young, fast-moving market can shift meaningfully within a single year in ways a single early conversation will not capture, and a founder who keeps listening after launch tends to catch a shift in taste well before it shows up in falling sales, which gives far more time to react than waiting for the numbers alone to tell the story.

The overlap is smaller than it looks. Imported beer competes on novelty and status at a price point most local taprooms cannot match, while craft beer competes on freshness and a direct relationship with the brewery. A new entrant chasing the imported shelf is usually fighting the wrong battle.
faqs: Is craft beer growing faster in metros or smaller cities?
Metros established the category first, but growth has been extending into tier-2 cities as state policy allows, though this varies significantly and unevenly by state.
Should a new brewery launch with cans or bottles?
Cans have been gaining share for retail packaging due to better protection in transit and lower shipping weight, though bottles remain common, particularly for premium positioning.
Are Indian drinkers moving away from mainstream styles?
Style range has been widening slowly, but mainstream lagers and approachable ales still make up most of the volume, so this is a gradual shift, not a completed one.
What is the most common way small breweries enter the Indian market?
Starting as a brewpub or taproom, on-trade first, has been the most common entry route, since it needs less packaging investment than launching straight into retail.
